  • Earlier in November, 17-year-old Kylie Arellano was rescued after secretly asking another player for help while playing Innersloth’s popular social deduction game.
  • Arellano had been missing since May 2025, when she disappeared from her home in Utah at the age of 15.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A 16-year-old boy has revealed how a chance encounter in Among Us led to him and his mother helping rescue a teenage girl who had allegedly been held captive for more than 500 days.

Earlier in November, 17-year-old Kylie Arellano was rescued after secretly asking another player for help while playing Innersloth’s popular social deduction game.

Arellano had been missing since May 2025, when she disappeared from her home in Utah at the age of 15. She was allegedly held against her will in the basement of a home in Huntington, Oregon.

For Colorado teenager Landon Tresp, what began as an ordinary gaming session on October 15 would end with him helping a girl hundreds of miles away escape her alleged captor.

After meeting in Among Us, Landon and Arellano struck up a friendship and began communicating through Discord.

“We just kind of clicked,” Landon mentioned.

Over the following two weeks, Arellano began opening up about her situation, eventually sending Landon news articles covering her disappearance.

Realizing something was seriously wrong, Landon turned to his mother, Khristina, for help on Halloween. Neither knew that within 24 hours, the girl would finally be free.

Khristina began speaking with Arellano through Discord, but locating the teenager proved challenging as she didn’t know the address where she was being held.

“I knew I had to do everything I could to make sure she was brought to safety and had a second chance,” Khristina recalled.

It has been revealed that determined to find her, Khristina searched online property records before turning to real estate website Zillow. After being sent photos of two potential houses, Arellano recognized the second property.

Teenage girl held captive for 500 days rescued after secretly asking for help in Among Us.

Among Us hackers targeted as InnerSloth rush out emergency hotfix.

World of Warcraft account helps police locate missing 16-year-old.

Khristina contacted the girl’s family and began working with the FBI to bring her home.

Speaking with KOAA, Khristina described how devastating it was to learn just how long Arellano had been missing.

“Just heartbreaking to think that she had been going through what she had for over 520 days and without anyone that she could reach a hand out to and not knowing where you’re at,” she mentioned.

On November 1, authorities arrived at the Oregon residence. Khristina stayed on a video call with Arellano, encouraging her to make the final few steps toward freedom.

Sources indicate that “I was on the video chat with her when I told her to face those basement stairs and run up them and down that hallway,” Khristina recalled. “And grab that front door because that was her freedom.”.

After more than 500 days away from home, Arellano was finally in the care of law enforcement and was taken for medical treatment and evaluation.

For Landon, seeing the friend he had met just weeks earlier finally reach safety was an overwhelming moment.

“Oh my God, just pure bliss. I was so happy she was safe in that car. I was so happy she was out of that horrible monster’s house,” he noted.

Sources indicate that adam Hunter Harmel, 39, has since been indicted on a federal charge of transportation with intent to engage in criminal sexual activity. Prosecutors allege he met the girl online before traveling to Utah and taking her across state lines.

Despite everything that happened, Landon and Arellano haven’t stopped playing video games together.

The pair remain friends, while Khristina continues to speak with Arellano every day. The family is also hoping to meet her in person.

What began with two strangers meeting in Among Us has become a friendship that extends far beyond the game, with Landon and his mother giving Arellano the help she had desperately needed for more than a year.

Fresh programmable photonic chip can control how fast light moves

📅 22 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1400 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers at Seoul National University and the University of Seoul have developed a programmable photonic integrated circuit that can slow light whenever needed.
  • The team was led by Professors Namkyoo Park and Sunkyu Yu of the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at Seoul National University, working with Professor Xianji Piao of the School of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the University of Seoul.
  • Slowing Light Could Help Solve a Computing Bottleneck.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers at Seoul National University and the University of Seoul have developed a programmable photonic integrated circuit that can slow light whenever needed.

The team was led by Professors Namkyoo Park and Sunkyu Yu of the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at Seoul National University, working with Professor Xianji Piao of the School of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the University of Seoul.

Slowing Light Could Help Solve a Computing Bottleneck.

In a recent development, the rapid growth of generative AI and large scale AI models has sharply increased the amount of computing power required by data centers and servers. Conventional electronic semiconductors are struggling to keep pace because they consume large amounts of energy and face limits in how quickly they can transmit data.

According to recent reports, these challenges have intensified interest in optical computing, which uses light rather than electrical signals to process information. Optical systems could potentially move data at extremely high speeds while using less power.

In a recent development, however, light also presents a major challenge. Because it naturally moves at a fixed speed, it is difficult to delay optical signals or temporarily hold them in place. Those capabilities are essential for creating buffers and memory functions in optical computers.

It has been revealed that to address this problem, the researchers designed a programmable photonic circuit that can control both the speed and shape of optical signals. Their approach provides more flexibility over "slow light" than previously proposed methods.

The study was published in the renowned international journal Advanced Science.

Why Optical Signals Sometimes Need To Wait.

Industry observers note that photonic integrated circuits are emerging as a promising technology for processing information promptly and efficiently with light. In data centers, optical communication networks, and future computing systems, moving signals rapidly is only part of the challenge.

Systems must also ensure that different signals arrive at the correct time. In some cases, a light signal must be delayed so it can remain synchronized with other information moving through the system.

One method for creating these delays relies on coupled-resonator-induced transparency (CRIT), which uses interference among several optical resonators.

CRIT allows light within a selected frequency range to pass through a device while also reducing the speed at which the optical signal travels.

Fixed Optical Devices Limit Flexibility.

Traditional CRIT devices usually have operating characteristics that become permanent once they are manufactured. This makes it difficult to change how they function after fabrication.

For example, engineers who want to create a longer signal delay or work with a different frequency range often need to design and manufacture an entirely new photonic device.

That lack of adaptability increases the complexity of optical communication hardware and data center infrastructure. It can also raise costs and extend development schedules whenever latest capabilities are needed.

Sources indicate that the problem is especially vital for AI servers and next-generation data centers, where enormous amounts of information must be processed in real time. Fixed optical components have therefore remained a major obstacle to more practical optical computing systems.

A Programmable Design for Controlling Light.

The research team developed a different strategy by treating two optical states in CRIT systems, known as the bright mode and dark mode, as one unified degree of freedom. The researchers also added two controllable loop couplers.

It has been revealed that together, these changes created a new design principle for programmable photonic integrated circuits. Resonator arrangements that were previously locked into one configuration after fabrication could instead be adjusted for different purposes.

Using the latest CRIT structure, the researchers showed that the movement of light could be delayed and controlled as needed. They also demonstrated that interference between the bright and dark modes could be handled as a single integrated design parameter.

This approach greatly expanded the flexibility of photonic resonator circuits that had previously been limited by fixed designs.

Controlling Delay, Bandwidth, and Signal Shape.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers theoretically demonstrated that the two loop couplers could be used to adjust the bandwidth and shape of the passband. They could also control how long signals were delayed and how efficiently those signals traveled through the circuit.

This means that both the speed and transmission behavior of optical signals could be reconfigured across entire systems containing multiple resonators, rather than only within a single resonator.

Numerical simulations also showed that the speed of optical pulses could be adjusted dynamically while the circuit was operating.

The results indicated that signal delay times could be changed without reducing processing performance. The system could also convert the frequency of light without requiring additional specialized components.

Simulations Suggest the Chip Could Be Practical.

The researchers used three-dimensional electromagnetic simulations to test whether the CRIT device could be built on a silicon nitride (Si3N4) photonic integrated circuit platform.

They also evaluated a range of real-world problems that could affect the device during manufacturing and operation. These included material losses, differences in resonator quality, backscattering, coupling fluctuations, phase errors in the loop couplers, and thermal crosstalk.

The simulations indicated that the proposed structure could continue to operate reliably under realistic conditions.

One Chip Could Perform Several Optical Functions.

The study introduces a programmable photonic platform that can control both the timing and frequency properties of light signals in real time.

Recent findings suggest that the design could overcome the limitations of conventional optical delay devices, which typically perform only fixed functions. It also suggests that several important capabilities could eventually be combined within one photonic circuit.

These functions include signal synchronization, adjustable delay lines, optical buffers, and frequency conversion.

The same design principles may also be useful beyond CRIT systems. The researchers believe the approach could be applied to a broad range of photonic circuits based on resonators, potentially providing a foundation for more adaptable optical signal processing technologies.

Potential Benefits for AI and Data Centers.

If the technology is commercialized, a single programmable optical chip could perform several tasks, including controlling signal speed and switching between different functions.

In that sense, the chip could operate in a way similar to a software-defined system, with its behavior adjusted according to changing needs.

This flexibility could help data centers and AI servers process information more efficiently while reducing energy consumption.

Combining several signal processing functions on one chip could also make optical communication equipment and sensor systems smaller and less expensive.

Over the longer term, the technology could support industries that depend on extremely fast information processing, including autonomous driving, next-generation communications, and quantum technologies.

Researchers Strategy Larger Programmable Photonic Systems.

Professor Namkyoo Park, co-corresponding author of the study from Seoul National University, stated, "This research is significant in that it proposes a fresh design principle that allows the flow of light within photonic integrated circuits to be reconfigured as needed, greatly enhancing design flexibility. We plan to expand this technology toward large-scale programmable photonic integrated circuits based on silicon photonics and photonic AI technologies.".

It has been revealed that co-first authors Dr. Seungkyun Park and Ph.D. student Beomjoon Chae, who led the theoretical framework and numerical analysis, added, "Through this study, we realized that reinterpreting conventional photonic resonator physics from a different perspective can serve as a starting point for discovering new functionalities in photonic integrated circuits. We strategy to further develop this research toward practical device implementation and experimental validation.".

Sources indicate that dr. Seungkyun Park is affiliated with the InnoCORE PICORE Center at KAIST and is at the moment conducting research on photonic AI and quantum optics at the Photonic Systems Laboratory, Seoul National University.

It has been revealed that ph.D. student Beomjoon Chae is conducting research on programmable photonic integrated circuits at the Intelligent Wave Systems Laboratory, SNU.

The research received support from the Ministry of Science and ICT through the Innovative Research Center (IRC) program, the Basic Research Laboratory (BRL) program, and the Young Researcher Program.

Dr. Seungkyun Park also participated in the study with support from the InnoCORE program (PICORE Center).

Over $60,000 has been raised to help cover the vet bills of a beloved railway station cat in England after he suddenly fell ill.

On November 23, a 12-year-old ginger cat known for greeting passengers at a train station in the UK was taken to the vet after his family noticed he was eating less and sleeping more than usual.

While George’s family is still waiting to find out what made their beloved pet unwell, feline fans from across the globe have shown their support by raising thousands of dollars to help with his treatment.

“George has brought so much happiness, laughter and comfort to so many people over the years, and now we’re doing everything we can to get him back to his happy, healthy self,” reads a post on the station cat’s Facebook page.

“We know times are difficult for so many, and your kind messages, love and good wishes mean more than you could possibly imagine…Thank you for loving our gorgeous ginger boy as much as we do. We’re keeping everything crossed for him.”.

In a post shared on George’s GoFundMe page, his family revealed that the cat’s medical bill has already reached $1,958 (£1,500), and mentioned that further investigations into the cat’s health could lead to further costs.

Recent findings suggest that however, since posting the campaign, George has received an outpouring of donations to help cover the costs. As of November 25, the cute cat has raised $60,582 (£46,393) of his $78,000 (£60,000) goal, much to the shock of his owners.

“We are completely overwhelmed and incredibly humbled by the love, kindness and generosity that has been shown towards our little ginger boy,” noted George’s social media manager Simone Carter.

George’s family has pledged to use any money left over after his medical bills are paid to help other cats in need.

“George has spent so many years bringing a little happiness into people’s lives, and it is incredibly moving to see just how much love is being returned to him,” noted Carter.

Industry observers note that suppose you don’t need the extra speed and capacity that Wi-Fi 7 offers, and you just want something cheap to give you decent coverage throughout your house? The Archer AX1450 is by no means a speed demon, delivering up to 250 Mbps over the 2.4 GHz band and up to 1,201 Mbps on the 5 GHz band. You can manage the Archer AX1450 with the usual webGUI on a desktop/laptop or use the TP-Link Tether app to control the router from your smartphone or tablet.

The Netgear RAX5 is a Wi-Fi 6 router with four GbE LAN ports and up to 1.6 Gbps aggregate wireless speeds across 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands.

Industry observers note that keep in mind that the RAX5 isn’t meant for homes that have a ton of smartphones, computers, and smart home devices. It only reliably supports up to 20 wireless devices. So if you have a desktop, a laptop, a couple of TVs, and a couple of smartphones, the RAX5 should do perfectly fine handling the load. If you have more demanding needs, step up to one of the best Wi-Fi 7 routers.

Sources indicate that as I previously mentioned, the TP-Link and Netgear routers are aimed at people who have less demanding wireless needs, and they’re priced to reflect this fact. They won’t win any throughput contests against their newer Wi-Fi 6E or Wi-Fi 7 competition, but those routers will also cost you around twice as much money.

#138786. Latest Update: MIT’s new lidar chip could give self-driving cars a wider view

Latest Update: MIT’s new lidar chip could give self-driving cars a wider view

📅 22 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1393 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Lidar technology uses pulses of infrared light to calculate distances and create detailed 3D maps of the surrounding environment.
  • It has been revealed that MIT researchers have now developed an approach that could lead to smaller, more durable lidar sensors that operate without any moving parts.
  • Sources indicate that existing lidar systems built with silicon-photonics chips usually have a narrow field of view.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lidar technology uses pulses of infrared light to calculate distances and create detailed 3D maps of the surrounding environment. This allows autonomous vehicles to detect objects in their path and respond promptly. However, conventional lidar sensors are often large and costly, and many rely on moving components that can wear out over time. These limitations make the systems difficult to use in a wider range of settings.

It has been revealed that MIT researchers have now developed an approach that could lead to smaller, more durable lidar sensors that operate without any moving parts. Their advance centers on a new silicon-photonics chip, a type of semiconductor device that controls light instead of electrical signals.

Sources indicate that existing lidar systems built with silicon-photonics chips usually have a narrow field of view. As a result, they struggle to scan areas located toward the edges of a scene. Previous attempts to expand this viewing range have often introduced extra noise and reduced measurement accuracy.

It has been revealed that the MIT team addressed those problems by creating an array of integrated antennas that greatly limits unwanted crosstalk, which occurs when neighboring antennas interfere with one another. The design allows the chip to scan across a broader field of view while producing less noise than other silicon-photonics-based methods.

A Smaller Lidar System With a Wider View.

The advance could support the development of more capable lidar sensors for challenging uses, including autonomous vehicle navigation, aerial mapping, and the monitoring of construction sites.

Industry observers note that "The functionality we demonstrated in this work solves a fundamental problem for integrated optical-phased-array technology, enabling future lidar sensors that can achieve significantly higher performance than we could demonstrate previously," says Jelena Notaros, the Robert J. Shillman Career Development Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) at MIT, a member of the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and senior author of a paper on this innovation.

Industry observers note that the study also includes lead author and EECS graduate student Henry Crawford-Eng, along with EECS graduate students Andres Garcia Coleto, Benjamin M. Mazur, Daniel M. DeSantis, and Tal Sneh. The findings were published recently in Nature Communications.

How Lidar Maps Its Surroundings.

Sources indicate that many traditional lidar systems use a large rotating unit to direct light pulses across a scene. When the light strikes nearby objects, it reflects back toward the sensor. The returning signals provide the information needed to reconstruct a detailed map of the environment.

According to recent reports, silicon-photonics-based lidar works differently. Rather than rotating a mechanical device, it scans a beam of light electronically in several directions with a system known as an integrated optical phased array (OPA).

According to recent reports, at the heart of an OPA is a group of integrated antennas. Each antenna contains tiny, regularly spaced variations along its length. These features, known as corrugations, cause light from an input source to scatter upward and out of the photonic chip.

Researchers can control the direction of the outgoing beam by changing the phase of the light sent to each antenna. Adjusting these phases changes the angle at which the array releases light, making it possible to steer the beam without moving any physical components.

Placing the antennas close together creates a serious obstacle. Neighboring antennas can couple with one another, scrambling the light they produce. Engineers have traditionally prevented this interference by increasing the distance between antennas, but wider spacing creates a different set of problems.

When antennas are too far apart, the array produces several copies of the same beam at different angles. The primary beam can only be moved a limited distance before it becomes difficult to distinguish from these additional copies.

"This limits our field of view, so the autonomous vehicle now only knows what is in front of it for a certain angular range," Garcia Coleto explains.

In a recent development, the unwanted beam copies, called grating lobes, can confuse the sensor and generate false detections. They also consume energy that could otherwise be directed into the main beam.

To overcome this tradeoff, the MIT researchers developed antennas with reduced crosstalk that can be positioned close together without strongly coupling.

Three Antenna Shapes Reduce Interference.

It has been revealed that in a conventional OPA, every antenna has an identical structure and uses the same pattern of corrugations. When these matching antennas are placed close together, they interact very strongly.

It has been revealed that the MIT team instead created a repeating set of three antennas with distinct shapes. They changed the width of the antennas as well as the size and placement of the corrugations. Because the antennas have different geometries, each one also has a different propagation coefficient, which describes how light moves through the structure.

"Because the antennas have very different propagation coefficients, when we put them close together, essentially each antenna doesn't 'see' the antenna next to it. Therefore, it won't couple with its neighbor," Garcia Coleto claims.

Making Different Antennas Behave the Same Way.

Sources indicate that reducing the coupling was only part of the challenge. Although the antennas needed different propagation coefficients, they still had to release light in the same consistent manner.

The team designed the antennas around three essential requirements.

Sources indicate that each antenna had to emit the same amount of light. Every antenna also needed to release its beam at the same angle when receiving the same wavelength. Finally, the angle of emission had to change evenly across the entire array as the beam was steered.

According to recent reports, "We have this challenge where we require the antennas to have different geometries to reduce the crosstalk, but we need to simultaneously design the antennas to have the same emission characteristics. While it is possible to engineer this, it is extremely difficult because, typically, when antennas are designed with different geometries, they tend to behave differently," Crawford-Eng says.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers began by developing the basic electromagnetic theory describing how radiative modes couple. They then used this theoretical framework to guide the design and computer simulation of the antennas.

Based on those calculations, the team manufactured an OPA containing the reduced-crosstalk antennas. The antennas were placed much closer together than those in a conventional system, and the completed device was then tested experimentally.

Interference Falls From About 100 Percent to 1 Percent.

In a recent development, under the conditions of the experiment, a typical OPA would have produced coupling of approximately 100 percent. The MIT design lowered that coupling to about 1 percent while still generating one clean and precise beam.

The system accurately steered the beam across a broad field of view without producing any grating lobes. This combination of wide scanning, low interference, and strong beam quality addresses one of the central obstacles facing integrated lidar technology.

The researchers now initiative to refine the method so the system can cover an even broader viewing range. They are also studying another possible approach to wide field-of-view performance that emerged while they were developing the underlying theory.

It has been revealed that "This work addresses a longstanding challenge in integrated optical phased arrays: simultaneously achieving both a wide field of view, which requires dense antenna spacing, and high beam quality, which requires low crosstalk between neighboring antennas. The authors solve this problem with an elegant antenna design. Their innovation is an important step forward for chip-scale, solid-state beam-steering technology," says Joyce Poon, professor of electrical and computer engineering at the University of Toronto and director of the Max Planck Institute of Microstructure Physics, who was not involved with this work.

Sources indicate that the Semiconductor Research Corporation, the National Science Foundation, an MIT MathWorks Fellowship, the U.S. Department of War, and the MIT Rolf G. Locher Endowed Fellowship supported the research, in part.

Some of the work was carried out using MIT.nano facilities.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rockstar Games has revealed several features that were scrapped during the development of GTA 6, including activities that were available in previous Grand Theft Auto games.

According to recent reports, after years of anticipation, GTA 6 has finally arrived, introducing players to Leonida alongside the franchise’s newest protagonists, Jason and Lucia. The game has also earned a Metacritic score of 99, matching The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

However, despite the number of activities available throughout the open world, Rockstar has revealed that several planned gameplay mechanics and returning features never made it into the finished game.

Speaking to German outlet PC Games, Rockstar North development manager Rob Nelson and design producer Scott Mitchell discussed several features that were considered during development but ultimately abandoned.

Industry observers note that among them was tennis, which players could participate in throughout GTA 5. Rockstar had planned to bring the activity back for GTA 6, but its implementation failed to meet the developer’s standards. Mini golf, however, made it into the finished game.

GTA 6 features that were cut, per a PC Games interview with Rob Nelson and Scott Mitchell of Rockstar North:Tennis (planned, but didn't meet Rockstar's standards)Cinema and theatre visits (not interactive enough)CrawlingHome decoratingCraftingSource:… pic.twitter.com/NviyEdt2M9.

Industry observers note that the developers also revealed that players were originally going to be able to crawl, decorate their homes, and craft items. These mechanics were ultimately scrapped, with some not fitting the game’s story or gameplay.

Cinema and theater visits were also removed, as Rockstar felt the activities were not interactive enough.

Nelson also explained how Red Dead Redemption 2 influenced the development of GTA 6, particularly when it came to storytelling and the relationship between its two protagonists.

The Western’s approach to pacing encouraged Rockstar to incorporate quieter moments into GTA 6, giving Jason and Lucia more opportunities for character development between the game’s action sequences.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The latest quarterly data for the US smartphone market reveals that Google Pixel is holding its ground despite the overall market faltering, and the other two major Android brands struggling.

The top smartphone brands in the United States include Apple, Samsung, Motorola, and Google Pixel in that order. Apple continues to absolutely dominate at a whopping 57% market share in Q3 2026, up from 50% during the same period last year.

Samsung came in at 25%, up 1% from last year (likely driven by a very successful Fold 8 launch during Q3), while Motorola shrank from 12% to 8%.

Google Pixel made up 6%, down 1% from Q3 2025, Counterpoint Research highlights. Q3 is important for Google as it includes the manufacturer’s new August release window for new flagships. It’s not surprising that Google dropped a percentage point year-over-year, as the company’s Pixel 11 launch was not particularly exciting, especially as prices rose over the previous generation. If anything, only dropping 1% must be pretty encouraging given the overall market conditions and RAMageddon of it all.

It has been revealed that something to note – Google Pixel is technically growing this year compared to last. Just out of view on this latest upgrade, Q2 2026 saw Google’s share up 1% year-over-year, and Q1 was also up compared to the same period in 2025. Counterpoint previously mentioned that the Pixel brand “remains aggressive in postpaid” carriers, but notes that Pixel 11 shipments were “weaker YoY.”.

Bark charges $15 per month for its proposal, which includes a Bark App subscription for the whole family. I also use the Bark App on my son’s phone, which helps me monitor his usage and make sure he’s safe online. The extra $5 per month adds up, but it’s absolutely worth it if you want to add the Bark App to another phone or tablet.

Industry observers note that the Bark Watch is fine enough for younger kids, but the design and lack of games feel more like an “older kids’ watch” to me, and my 12-year-old son agrees. Either way you go, these are fantastic choices that you’ll be happy with, especially with a nice little deal.

Latest Update: World’s first superconducting quantum heat engine could help unlock massive quantum computers

📅 14 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (839 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A newly developed superconducting quantum heat engine could deepen our understanding of thermodynamics while helping advance technologies needed for quantum computers with very large numbers of qubits.
  • Industry observers note that scientists are getting a clearer picture of how thermodynamics behaves in the quantum world, and that progress could benefit both quantum technology and our understanding of familiar thermodynamic principles.
  • In a recent development, the experiment connects two areas of physics that normally describe very different scales.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly developed superconducting quantum heat engine could deepen our understanding of thermodynamics while helping advance technologies needed for quantum computers with very large numbers of qubits.

Industry observers note that scientists are getting a clearer picture of how thermodynamics behaves in the quantum world, and that progress could benefit both quantum technology and our understanding of familiar thermodynamic principles. Researchers at Aalto University have now taken an important step by demonstrating the first cyclic quantum heat engine built inside a superconducting circuit.

In a recent development, the experiment connects two areas of physics that normally describe very different scales. Quantum mechanics explains the behavior of matter at extremely small scales, even below the size of atoms, while thermodynamics describes how heat and energy behave in much larger systems, from collections of molecules to the universe itself. Bringing the two together raises a fundamental question: what happens to familiar thermodynamic processes when quantum effects such as tunneling, entanglement, and superposition enter the picture?

A Heat Engine Built for the Quantum World.

It has been revealed that conventional heat engines turn heat into useful work. James Watt's steam engine is one famous example, but the same basic concept remains central to modern transportation and electricity production, powering cars, ships, planes and many power plants.

The researchers have now created the world's first superconducting quantum heat engine. The extremely small device combines a transmon qubit, a resonator and a quantum refrigerator.

It has been revealed that operating under ultracold quantum conditions, the engine was able to use the tiny amount of available heat to repeatedly produce positive work. Achieving this kind of cyclic operation has been an key objective for researchers working on quantum heat engines. The result provides a proof of concept for superconducting heat engines that could eventually contribute to improved quantum computing technology.

The study, led by Academy Professor Mikko Möttönen, was published in Nature Communications.

Recreating an Otto Cycle Near Absolute Zero.

Industry observers note that to make the engine operate, the researchers reproduced an Otto cycle inside a superconducting circuit. The Otto cycle is a thermodynamic process also used in car engines and other conventional machines.

"In our experiment, we built a nanofabricated heat engine using superconducting circuits and operated it in a cryostat near absolute zero. At its heart is a transmon qubit, one of the basic building blocks of modern quantum technologies," says Tuomas Uusnäkki, the study's first author.

The researchers connected the transmon qubit to a quantum circuit refrigerator, allowing them to control heat flow on the quantum scale and demonstrate that this heat could be transformed into measurable work. A conventional heat engine normally relies on separate hot and cold environments. In this system, however, the same quantum refrigerator can supply both heating and cooling.

"Our quantum-circuit refrigerator can be tuned to both heat and cool the qubit on demand. Using carefully timed control pulses, we drove the engine in an Otto cycle and monitored the qubit state as the engine ran," explains Uusnäkki.

Measurements showed that heat passing through the qubit during the cycle was producing positive work.

"This is the first experimental demonstration of a cyclic quantum heat engine in superconducting circuits. Using a single controllable quantum refrigerator as both the hot and cold environment of the engine makes it simpler and more versatile," says Uusnäkki.

Toward Autonomous Quantum Computer Hardware.

According to recent reports, the researchers are now trying to improve the design and eventually develop a fully autonomous heat engine. One possible use would be reading out qubits without having to carry a microwave pulse from millikelvin temperatures all the way to room temperature.

Recent findings suggest that that capability could become especially valuable as quantum computers grow. Autonomous devices integrated directly into superconducting circuits could reduce both the cost and complexity of machines containing very large numbers of qubits.

"Finland's Quantum Technology Strategy envisions a quantum computer with one thousand logical qubits by 2035, which probably means hundreds of thousands of physical qubits. Doing that with current technology requires millions of microwave cables costing thousand euros each. The cables also introduce noise into the system. Using autonomous devices instead would mostly eliminate the need for those cables," Möttönen says.

Reducing the need for those microwave connections could therefore address two challenges at once: the enormous hardware requirements of large quantum computers and the unwanted noise that cables can introduce into quantum systems.

The pioneering experiment was carried out using OtaNano, Finland's national research infrastructure for nano, micro and quantum technology. Funding came from the Research Council of Finland and the Finnish Cultural Foundation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clicks is still on track to release the phone with a physical keyboard within the next few months, but a Communicator launch before the end of this year isn’t looking very likely as shipping gets pushed back.

Sources indicate that the Communicator is a fresh take on what an Android phone can be. It was first introduced at CES earlier this year, with the main selling angle being the physically integrated keyboard. Clicks wants to target those who are looking for a second device, and the Communicator fits the bill.

Last we heard, the Clicks Communicator was on track to launch and ship in December, following a cheery revision detailing an upgrade to 12GB of RAM and other changes. However, Clicks posted a new update today stating that the timeline has shifted out a month because of supply chain issues caused by something other than RAM.

Unfortunately, we’ve encountered a delay with securing a critical supply chain component needed to fabricate our printed circuit board ahead of manufacturing and final assembly. Assembly will now begin in early January, with deliveries expected to start in late January.

It notes that the “critical supply chain component” is the essential fabric used for the company’s printed circuit boards. The blog post dives into some neat details about the component holding things up. The PCBs Clicks is using are made up of more material layers than some competitor boards. But the fabric used to layer those boards is in short supply at this sort of demand, with four manufacturers reportedly unable to meet the company’s required volume.

Recent findings suggest that the post also spells out difficulties caused by troubles in the Middle East, and rising memory costs straining the chain of supply further, even if memory – surprisingly – isn’t the cause of this small delay. Those compounded issues have pushed production back, and users are now told to expect their Clicks Communicator pre-orders to be shipped in late January, at the earliest. Many pre-orders will likely be shipped after that because of further time constraints before Chinese Fresh Year.

In an act of good faith, Clicks says it’s including a set of 3.5mm wired headphones in each box for orders placed prior to today.

It has been revealed that A push from December to January isn’t massive, and Clicks still seems to be making solid time on developing a form factor we don’t often see. You can still pre-order the Clicks Communicator starting at $649.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A GTA 6 player has created a website that allows anyone to play Rockstar Games’ latest release for free by remotely taking control of their PS5.

While GTA 6 is presently available on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S, those without either console have been left waiting for Rockstar to bring the game to PC.

However, a website called PlayMyPS5 is giving players another way to experience Vice City without having to purchase the game or a console, while attempting to get the internet to complete its story together.

PlayMyPS5 broadcasts gameplay directly from a physical PS5, allowing visitors to join a public queue and remotely control the console through their web browser.

Industry observers note that each player is given five minutes to play before control is handed over to the next person in line. Players have 20 seconds to claim their turn, while remaining idle for 30 seconds will bring their session to an early end.

The website supports controllers, keyboard and mouse, and mobile touchscreen controls. Players can also watch others explore Vice City and communicate through a live chat while waiting for their turn.

There are no downloads, payments, or registration requirements to join the queue, and players can rejoin once their session ends.

It has been revealed that the project was created after its developers realized their PS5 spent much of its time sitting unused. Now, they’re encouraging visitors to work together to complete every GTA 6 story mission.

The creators are also attempting to raise $993 to purchase a second PS5, allowing more people to play simultaneously and reducing queue times. Other PS5 owners with a copy of GTA 6 can volunteer to share their consoles through the platform.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A Finnish study has found an unexpected association between screen use and cognitive performance. Children who accumulated more screen time as they grew up tended to show better cognitive processing during adolescence. One of the researchers cautions against viewing screen time as entirely harmful and says the goal should be to balance physical activity with screen use that encourages active thinking.

Low levels of physical activity among adolescents remain a significant public health concern. Sedentary behavior has been associated with poorer academic achievement, while physical activity is known to support brain function, particularly in adults. Much less is known, however, about how physical activity and sedentary behavior during childhood and adolescence relate to cognitive processing later in adolescence.

These years are especially vital because the brain is still developing. Factors that shape cognitive abilities during childhood and adolescence may have lasting effects that extend into adulthood, potentially influencing education and working life.

Industry observers note that researchers examined how physical activity, sedentary behavior, and screen time from childhood through adolescence were related to cognitive processing in the teenage years. They also looked for differences between girls and boys and investigated whether the intensity of physical activity played a role.

More Screen Time Linked to Better Cognitive Processing.

The results showed that greater screen time beginning in childhood was associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.

It has been revealed that "The findings suggest that screen time can support children's and adolescents' cognitive processing. Presumably, the essential point here is what kind of things they do in their screen time. Teachers and parents should encourage children to use devices and screens in such ways that promote active thinking, problem-solving, creativity and learning," states Doctoral Researcher Petri Jalanko from the University of Jyväskylä.

Recent findings suggest that the findings suggest that the type of screen activity may be important. Digital activities that involve learning, creativity, problem-solving, or other forms of active mental engagement could potentially help explain the association observed in the study.

"We should not regard screen time solely as harmful but seek balance between physical activity and screen time that promotes active thinking," Jalanko summarizes.

Physical Activity Showed Different Links in Girls and Boys.

The relationship between physical activity and cognition was more complicated.

Recent findings suggest that among girls, greater amounts of light intensity physical activity since childhood were associated with better working memory during adolescence. Among boys, greater participation in guided physical activity from childhood through adolescence was linked to better working memory.

Industry observers note that the researchers also found an unexpected pattern involving unsupervised exercise. Lower levels of self-reported unsupervised physical activity were associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.

Industry observers note that by contrast, physical activity and sedentary time measured using a device that tracked heart rate and movement were not associated with cognitive processing. One possible explanation is that these sensors can measure movement and physiological activity but cannot determine exactly what a person is doing during periods of activity or inactivity.

"Our study indicates that the connections of physical activity and sedentary behavior to cognitive processing are complex and depend on the sex, the type and assessment method of physical activity and sedentary time. Moreover, boys and girls may benefit from different types of physical activity in view of brain health," Jalanko adds.

More Research Is Needed to Determine Cause and Effect.

The researchers emphasize that the findings show associations rather than proving that screen time or particular types of physical activity directly cause changes in cognitive performance.

According to recent reports, "However, we need more intervention studies to find out causal relations and sex differences in this respect. Moreover, it is notable to examine more specifically the effects of the intensity of physical activity on changes taking place in cognitive processing.".

The results come from an eight-year follow-up of the PANIC study on children's physical activity and nutrition. The current analysis included 124 girls and 136 boys with an average age of 15.8 years.

Recent findings suggest that researchers measured physical activity and sedentary behavior using both survey questionnaires and a device that combined heart rate and movement measurements. Learning, attention, and working memory were evaluated using the CogState test battery.

The research was published in the journal Pediatric Exercise Science.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An Uber Eats driver in Massachusetts helped save an elderly woman after hearing her faint cries for help while attempting to complete a delivery.

Brandon McSorley had started delivering orders through Uber Eats to earn extra money ahead of the holiday season when he received an order from a customer in Carver on November 22.

The delivery took him to Cranberry Village, a residential community for people aged 55 and older, where he noticed something was wrong after arriving at the customer’s home.

McSorley told CBS News that the woman had ordered Tylenol and ginger ale. Because the delivery contained medication, he was required to verify the customer’s ID before handing over the order.

Industry observers note that however, the house was dark when he arrived, and nobody answered the door. After waiting several minutes and attempting to contact the customer, he began hearing noises from inside the residence.

Industry observers note that “I could hear, like, a faint calling. I thought it was potentially someone telling me to go away or something like that,” he remarked.

Industry observers note that mcSorley remained outside until the woman’s cries became clearer, allowing him to hear her asking for help after suffering a fall. He immediately called 911 and waited for emergency services to arrive.

Recent findings suggest that first responders transported the woman to a nearby hospital. According to Carver EMS, she had been lying on the floor for approximately 45 minutes without access to a phone or a medical alert device.

Carver EMS Chief Michael Ryan credited the delivery driver’s actions with preventing the woman from potentially spending much longer on the floor.

Speaking to WCVB 5, McSorley noted he was grateful that his delivery had brought him to the woman’s home when it did.

“Just, right place at the right time. I’m glad I could be there and really do something to help.”.

It’s not clear how massive of a tip McSorley received from the whole ordeal, but he surely earned a five-star review.

Latest Update: Tiny robots powered by light can hunt down and collect bacteria

📅 18 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (655 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, robots small enough to operate in the microbial world could give scientists a fresh way to directly handle objects that are impossible to manipulate by hand.
  • Recent findings suggest that that capability could be especially useful for biological materials in water, including individual cells and bacteria.
  • One of the biggest obstacles in developing machines this small is finding an effective way to propel and control them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, robots small enough to operate in the microbial world could give scientists a fresh way to directly handle objects that are impossible to manipulate by hand. These tiny machines are around 50 times smaller than the diameter of a human hair, bringing researchers closer to the long-pursued goal of interacting directly with the microscopic world.

Recent findings suggest that that capability could be especially useful for biological materials in water, including individual cells and bacteria. Precisely controlling and moving objects at this scale has been a persistent challenge. The newly developed nanorobots show that it is already possible to collect bacteria, transport them, and release them at selected locations.

Light Powers and Steers the Tiny Robots.

One of the biggest obstacles in developing machines this small is finding an effective way to propel and control them. At Julius-Maximilians-Universität Würzburg (JMU), a research team led by Professor Bert Hecht has been developing a solution that uses the recoil produced by individual photons to move microscopic devices known as microdrones.

In a recent development, the devices contain as many as four plasmonic nanoantennas. These antennas absorb light with a particular color and helicity, then emit that light in a specific direction. Redirecting each photon creates a tiny recoil force, similar in principle to the recoil produced when a bullet is fired. Because the microdrones have so little mass, those extremely small forces can generate substantial acceleration and speed.

It has been revealed that for the latest work, the researchers reduced the size of their light-powered robots even further, producing devices smaller than one micrometer. Simplifying the steering system was an key part of achieving that size while retaining propulsion based on photon recoil.

The newly introduced control method takes advantage of nanoscale antenna wires built into the robot. These wires naturally tend to align with the polarization direction of incoming light. By changing the light's polarization, the researchers can control which direction the nanorobot faces. At the same time, photon recoil continues to propel it forward, creating a steering system that works somewhat like the directional control used in larger vehicles.

Nanorobots Act as "Microscopic Cleaners".

According to recent reports, "In essence, we have built a light-driven nanorobot that can track down and collect bacteria," claims Jin Qin, lead experimental scientist of the study. "By simplifying the design, we reached a size at which these robots can operate directly in the microbial world - almost like microscopic cleaning devices.".

Recent findings suggest that the robots are also highly maneuverable. They can make extremely fast 90° turns, helping them scan broad areas of a sample in an organized and efficient way. They can also selectively capture, carry, and release substantial numbers of bacteria.

Industry observers note that under controlled laboratory conditions, this means the nanorobots can effectively "clean" microscopic environments. They gather bacteria from one area and deposit them at specifically chosen locations.

Sources indicate that "This is a striking example of how light can be used not only to observe the microscopic world, but also to actively shape it," adds Bert Hecht. "The idea of tiny robotic cleaners may sound futuristic, but we are already demonstrating the physical principles that make it possible.".

The robots remain fully maneuverable even while carrying larger groups of bacteria, although their speed decreases somewhat under the added load. That ability to keep functioning while transporting larger bacterial clusters points to possible future uses in microbiology, biomedical research, and precise manipulation of materials at the microscopic scale.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Animal rights organization PETA is urging Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to ditch his iconic black leather jacket, even sending the billionaire an $875 vegan alternative made from olive waste.

Much like Steve Jobs with his black turtlenecks and Mark Zuckerberg with his gray T-shirts, Huang’s leather jackets have become synonymous with the Nvidia boss.

His signature look has even proven lucrative. In July 2026, one of Huang’s signed Tom Ford leather jackets sold for a staggering $960,000 at auction, fetching 16 times its estimated price.

However, following Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO amid an ongoing foreign intelligence investigation for cheating on his wife with an alleged Chinese spy, PETA wants the billionaire to give his wardrobe an upgrade.

In a November 18 letter addressed to Huang, PETA President Tracy Reiman argued that despite his reputation as a technological innovator, his fashion choices were outdated.

“Tech doesn’t move forward by clinging to outdated systems, and neither does fashion,” Reiman said. “PETA is calling on everyone to embrace vegan leathers made from cactus, cork, apples, and other plant materials and leave animals out of their wardrobes.”.

To encourage Huang to make the switch, PETA sent him an $875 jacket from fashion brand Benedetti Life, according to the New York Post.

The jacket is made using Oleatex, a leather alternative derived from olive harvesting waste. It features an organic cotton lining and an exterior consisting of 95% Biotex and 5% polyurethane.

PETA has also asked Huang to donate his old leather jacket to its planned Museum of Animal-Sourced Atrocities, offering the billionaire the prospect of a tax deduction in return.

Sources indicate that whether Huang is willing to part ways with his extensive leather jacket collection remains to be seen. The Nvidia boss previously revealed that he owns between 30 and 40 of them.

We've recommended the AudioEngine A2+ speakers for years, and the newer A2 GEN3 speakers only make them better. As usual, these speakers feature a 2.75-inch woofer and 0.75-inch tweeter, and they're among the best-sounding speakers in this class. The Creative Labs Pebble V2 is a set of stereo speakers that connect to your PC via USB and feature a minimalist design.

The Creative Labs Pebble V2 speakers are a go-to recommendation for cheap PC speakers here at Tom's Hardware, and for good reason. As you can read about in our review of the larger Creative Pebble Pro speakers, this range offers plenty of headroom, providing clean sound at higher volumes despite the tiny woofer size (just two inches). Like many Bluetooth speakers, the Pebble V2 set features passive radiators, capturing low-end frequencies to give the impression of a subwoofer. Of course, it's not the same as a subwoofer, but passive bass chambers help a lot with these smaller speakers.

You connect the speakers over a 3.5mm cable for audio, and power them with USB-C (the speakers call for a 10W port). RMS power here is 16W, giving you significantly more headroom at higher volumes to avoid any distortion. The 2.75-inch full range drivers offers decent low-end, though the frequency response cuts off just below 100 Hz, leaving precious sub-region frequencies out of the sonic picture. That gives you a good cutoff point to add a subwoofer, however.

The speakers can output via USB-C, Bluetooth 5.3, or a 3.5mm, and they come with included stands, which is something even AudioEngine lacks.

This desktop speaker includes dual four-inch drivers, as well as an integrated EQ and wireless remote.

If you're looking for maximum power, you get 120W of goodness with Edifier's S1000MKII speakers, which are on sale for $100 off right now. These are large speakers with 5.5-inch aluminum alloy drivers and 1-inch titanium dome tweeters.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra’s main advantages over the Galaxy S26 and S26+ are Privacy Display, the integrated S Pen, and its more versatile camera hardware.

Having different lenses gives you more options for portraits, travel photos, and subjects you can’t easily walk closer to.

The regular Galaxy S26 is the more natural choice if you prioritize a smaller phone and a lower purchase price. The Galaxy S26+ makes sense if you want a large-screen Galaxy without paying for Ultra-specific features.

The biggest improvement since launch is the move from Android 16-based One UI 8.5 to Android 17-based One UI 9.

Samsung has also made Smart Switch even better, which allows you to rapidly and easily port over your apps, data, and media from another device.

#138767. Scientists turn DNA into a memory device that uses 100x less power

Scientists turn DNA into a memory device that uses 100x less power

📅 17 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1220 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • DNA serves as the genetic blueprint for every living organism, but it is also an extraordinarily dense way to store information.
  • In a recent development, the challenge has been finding a way to make biological DNA function effectively alongside electronic materials.
  • The work, published in Advanced Functional Materials and the subject of a patent application, relies on two key components.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

DNA serves as the genetic blueprint for every living organism, but it is also an extraordinarily dense way to store information. A single gram can hold about 215 million gigabytes of data. Bringing that remarkable storage capacity into electronics could lead to more efficient data centers, faster processing and systems capable of handling increasingly complex information.

In a recent development, the challenge has been finding a way to make biological DNA function effectively alongside electronic materials. Penn State researchers have now developed an approach designed to overcome that incompatibility.

The work, published in Advanced Functional Materials and the subject of a patent application, relies on two key components. One is synthetic DNA, made from commercially available, chemically engineered molecules arranged into short genetic sequences tailored for specific electronic requirements. The other is crystalline perovskite, a semiconductor already used in technologies including solar cells, lasers and data storage devices.

Sources indicate that "Biology and electronics are different domains," remarked Kavya S. Keremane, co-corresponding author and postdoctoral researcher in materials science and engineering at Penn State. "Bridging these two fields required developing an entirely upcoming materials platform that allows them to function seamlessly together. By combining the information storage capabilities of DNA with the exceptional electronic properties of perovskite semiconductors, we created a bio-hybrid system that fundamentally changes how low-power memory devices can be designed.".

Building a Low Power Memory Device.

Sources indicate that using these materials, the team created a memory resistor, known as a "memristor," that operates with very little energy. Unlike ordinary resistors, which maintain a set resistance to electrical current in devices ranging from cell phones to space shuttles and lose their stored information when power disappears, memristors can preserve a record of previous electrical activity. They can remember the direction in which current previously flowed even after the power source is removed.

Industry observers note that that ability allows information to be stored and processed in the same place, resembling the way neurons function in the brain. Such an arrangement could support more simultaneous and sophisticated forms of data processing. According to the researchers, however, practical commercial systems would still require enough storage capacity and electrical power to become costly and inefficient without DNA's ability to pack enormous amounts of information into a very small space while consuming little energy.

"As the demand for artificial intelligence (AI) grows, we need a new strategy for low-power, high-storage devices," mentioned Bed Poudel, co-corresponding author and research professor of materials science and engineering at Penn State.

Recent findings suggest that poudel said AI and other emerging technologies are expected to depend increasingly on neuromorphic computing, which is designed to operate more like the human brain. Such systems can evaluate multiple inputs at once while making decisions informed by previous experiences and future priorities.

Recent findings suggest that "Usually, it takes more power to store more information. Our device, however, consumes 100 times less power and the storage capacity is higher than traditional storage devices, like flash drives.".

Engineering DNA to Conduct Electricity.

To construct the device, the researchers added silver nanoparticles to a layer of customized DNA sequences -- specially designed to be of certain compositions and lengths -- that was integrated with thin films of perovskite.

Recent findings suggest that this technique, called "doping," involves introducing a small amount of another material to produce specific properties. In this case, adding the silver nanoparticles allowed the DNA to conduct electricity while also helping its molecular units line up in a more orderly arrangement.

Synthetic DNA offered another important advantage over natural DNA. Unlike natural DNA -- long, entangled strands that behave like wet spaghetti when handled -- short and rigid pieces of synthetic DNA can be arranged with much greater precision at extremely small scales.

According to co-author Neela H. Yennawar, research professor and director of the Penn State Huck Institutes of the Life Sciences' Biomolecular Interactions Core Facility, molecularly engineered DNA can provide structural organization, adjustable electrical conductivity and functional control that natural DNA cannot achieve when incorporated into thin films.

"We can computationally determine exactly which sequences we need and how long they should be, and then we can rationally design them with synthetic DNA," Yennawar said. "These structures can be systematically doped with silver and other ions and engineered to interface seamlessly with perovskites -- transforming DNA from a biological macromolecule into a programmable, multifunctional nanomaterials platform.".

DNA and Perovskite Work Better Together.

When combined, the silver-doped DNA and perovskite formed bio-hybrid pathways that directed the flow of electrical current through the device.

It has been revealed that the researchers found that electrons moved reliably when they applied less than 0.1 volt -- for comparison, standard U.S. outlets have 120 volts -- and the device responded predictably when the direction of the current was changed.

Recent findings suggest that the carefully designed DNA structures, combined with the perovskite, also helped make the device unusually stable. According to the team, it continued operating consistently at temperatures approaching 250 degrees Fahrenheit and remained functional at room temperature for more than six weeks, substantially exceeding the performance standards of existing perovskite-based memory storage devices.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers also reported that the newly introduced system could perform the same memory function as comparable technologies while consuming only one-tenth as much power. That level of efficiency could make the approach especially attractive for future electronics designed to handle large amounts of information with lower energy demands.

Recent findings suggest that "Using just the DNA or just perovskite alone did not produce near as robust a result as the combination," Keremane said. "It's this combination that enables a very high memory storage density that requires very little power.".

A Upcoming Direction for Bio-Inspired Electronics.

The team now aims to improve the technology further and explore additional uses for bio-inspired electronic systems.

In a recent development, "Nature has the solution -- we just have to find it and apply it," Poudel said. "This work of integrating DNA into electronics to do amazing things gives a glimpse into what is possible.".

Recent findings suggest that in addition to Keremane, Yennawar and Poudel, other Penn State co-authors include co-corresponding author Luyao Zheng, postdoctoral research in materials science and engineering; Haodong Wu, doctoral student in materials science and engineering; Jiamao Zheng, who was a master's student in materials science and engineering at the time of research and has since graduated from Penn State; Shashank Priya, who was a professor of materials science and engineering at the time of research; and Chiranth C. Ravi, who was a master's student in the Huck Institutes of the Life Sciences at the time of research and has since graduated from Penn State. Abhinav Gorthy and co-corresponding author Rashmi Jha, chemical engineering and materials science, University of Minnesota, also contributed.

The U.S. National Science Foundation, the National Institutes of Health, Penn State and the University of Minnesota supported this research.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google’s Fitbit Air is one of my favorite products of 2026 and my preferred workout companion, but not being able to see a workout while you’re in the middle of it has been a huge complaint of mine, and the latest Google Health enhancement is fixing that.

Quite literally at the start of this week, I was on a walk through my neighborhood and though to myself, “it’s still pretty annoying that I can’t see my workout progress in the Google Health app.” It’s been a complaint of mine for a while, as various treadmill sessions and more have left me wondering what my heart rate is looking like, how many steps I’ve taken, etc, and it’s only a problem when using the Fitbit Air, seeing as the Pixel Watch (or Fitbit Edge) I’d wear otherwise will show that data front and center.

Google Health 5.13 is fixing that.

In a recent development, in the changelog for Google Health 5.13, Google details a newly introduced “exercise in-progress” card on the main “Today” screen. This will show what exercise is being tracked and also let you end the workout early.

If you use your Pixel Watch, Fitbit Air, or Fitbit Edge to automatically track your exercises, you’ll now see an exercise-in-progress card on your mobile app’s Today screen. This card lets you know that your device is tracking your exercise and gives you the opportunity to end the tracking and get your summary whenever you want.

We don’t know exactly what this card looks like just yet, but it sounds like it fits the need perfectly.

Google Health 5.13 is now rolling out on Android and iOS.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A 103-year-old gaming grandmother is taking part in a Tekken tournament, with one of her closest rivals also being 95 years old.

It has been revealed that even though gaming, and especially esports, are seen as a hobby for the younger generation, there are plenty of older folks who get involved as well. Those who grew up on the likes of the PlayStation One, Atari 2600, NES, and even the Sega Genesis still want to be involved.

Over in Japan, the Care Esports Association runs competitive gaming events aimed at senior citizens throughout the year, with an annual event taking place in December around Tekken 8.

Typically, competitors are aged between 70 and 90, but this year, they’ve cracked the 100-year-old mark, with a 103-year-old grandmother taking part.

As per Denfaminico, 103-year-old Toshiko Morishita will play in this year’s event, which is also looking to set a Guinness World Record for the “highest average age of esports tournament participants.”.

According to the outlet, the 103-year-old knows that her age might be a barrier to success, but said that even losing would still be “enjoyable” for her.

She “enjoys the game” without “being solely focused on winning or losing,” but has been putting in practice to prepare for the event.

As noted, competitors at the event typically range from 70 to 90 years old, with last year’s winner – Hisako Sakai – clocking in at 92 years old.

Sakai fought her way to first place using Claudio Serafino and defeated 95-year-old Sadayuki Kato in the semifinals.

The average age at last year’s event was just under 87, so having a 103-year-old competing will drag that up – hopefully, for them, into Guinness World Records territory.

On the other end of the scale, a five-year-old Tekken player drew attention for playing in a tournament, seeing as the game is rated for teenagers. Harada gave him a pass, though, saying he has a “bright future.”.

NASA just used satellites and debris to navigate without GPS

📅 26 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (777 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • NASA's Starling mission has reached another milestone in autonomous spaceflight by demonstrating a system that can determine a satellite's orbital position using other objects in space as reference points rather than depending on an external navigation network.
  • The technology, called FALCON (Fast Autonomous Lost-in-space Catalog-based Optical Navigation), is designed to help spacecraft operate with greater independence.
  • Satellites near Earth commonly rely on GPS for navigation, but those signals may be weak, unreliable, or unavailable around the Moon and in deep space.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA's Starling mission has reached another milestone in autonomous spaceflight by demonstrating a system that can determine a satellite's orbital position using other objects in space as reference points rather than depending on an external navigation network.

The technology, called FALCON (Fast Autonomous Lost-in-space Catalog-based Optical Navigation), is designed to help spacecraft operate with greater independence. Such capabilities could become increasingly important as NASA pursues missions farther from Earth, including lunar satellite swarms, distributed science missions, and future human exploration.

Satellites near Earth commonly rely on GPS for navigation, but those signals may be weak, unreliable, or unavailable around the Moon and in deep space. FALCON offers an alternative by allowing spacecraft to determine where they are using what they can observe around them.

The FALCON payload is a joint flight experiment developed by NASA and EraDrive, a startup that emerged from Stanford University. The system combines EraDrive's Era-Core flight software and embedded algorithms with Starling's cameras and an onboard catalog of known satellites. Together, these tools enable GPS-independent navigation while also helping the spacecraft track activity and objects in its surroundings.

It has been revealed that "FALCON is yet another success for the Starling demonstration mission. The results from FALCON can have far-reaching implications for on-orbit space-traffic monitoring, collision avoidance, and alternative navigation," said Roger Hunter, program manager for NASA's Small Spacecraft and Distributed Systems program at NASA's Ames Research Center in California's Silicon Valley. "The number of 'firsts' from Starling just keeps growing.".

Using Satellites and Debris as Reference Points.

In a recent development, the FALCON demonstration evaluated two related capabilities using Starling's onboard star tracker cameras. These cameras are standard spacecraft instruments that detect bright objects in space and help determine a spacecraft's orientation and position.

During position, navigation, and timing experiments, FALCON identified objects seen by Starling's cameras, including other spacecraft and orbital debris, and compared them with a publicly available catalog of known space objects maintained by the U.S. Department of War. Once the observed objects were identified and verified, FALCON used them as reference points to calculate Starling's orbit.

According to recent reports, A separate set of experiments tested whether the spacecraft could improve orbital estimates for the objects it observed. Mission controllers loaded a catalog containing approximately 20,000 space objects and their predicted orbits onto Starling.

Over a period of three days, FALCON improved the known orbits of more than 200 objects without any intervention from operators on the ground.

A First for Autonomous Optical Navigation.

FALCON's ability to determine its own orbit represents a first for a spacecraft navigating with optical cameras based on its position relative to other objects in space. In separate catalog updating tests, Starling also generated better onboard predictions of object positions than those supplied by ground stations.

Industry observers note that these abilities could be especially valuable for future networks of satellites operating without GPS. Coordinated satellite systems may play an important role in supporting human activities on the surfaces of the Moon or Mars.

Recent findings suggest that precise spacecraft positioning is also essential for distributed science missions, where measurements collected from several locations in space must be accurately aligned. For space traffic management, autonomous navigation and onboard catalog updates could reduce dependence on ground-based tracking networks while improving collision avoidance.

From University Research to Commercial Technology.

Recent findings suggest that the FALCON experiment also demonstrates NASA's role in helping university research develop into commercial technology. The work began as a University SmallSat Technology Partnerships project before developing into EraDrive, which is now commercializing its Era-Core software and related hardware for wider use.

Starling gave the technology an opportunity to be tested under real conditions in orbit, demonstrating how advanced flight software can allow satellites to function as increasingly autonomous navigators.

Industry observers note that later this year, Starling, which debuted in 2023, will expand the FALCON experiment using Era-Core. The mission's four spacecraft will share tracking information with one another and use those combined observations to refine their positions collectively.

According to recent reports, NASA's Ames Research Center in California's Silicon Valley leads the Starling mission. NASA's Small Spacecraft and Distributed Systems program, based at Ames and within the Research and Technology Mission Directorate, funds and manages the Starling mission.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Japan is expanding its AI crackdown on manga and anime piracy overseas after testing a system that can find websites hosting unauthorized copies.
  • According to recent reports, on November 24, The Yomiuri Shimbun reported that Japan’s Agency for Cultural Affairs found pirated manga on 94% of the 1,935 websites its AI flagged for suspected manga piracy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Japan is expanding its AI crackdown on manga and anime piracy overseas after testing a system that can find websites hosting unauthorized copies.

According to recent reports, on November 24, The Yomiuri Shimbun reported that Japan’s Agency for Cultural Affairs found pirated manga on 94% of the 1,935 websites its AI flagged for suspected manga piracy. Of the 1,564 sites flagged for suspected anime piracy, 89% hosted unauthorized copies.

For its overseas tests, the agency trained the AI to recognize domain names commonly associated with piracy sites and could compile the results as early as March 2027.

Japan’s latest anti-piracy push follows an April 3 discussion in the country’s House of Representatives, where executives from some of Japan’s biggest animation studios warned that piracy remains one of the biggest obstacles to anime’s growth overseas.

Among them was Toei Animation, the studio behind One Piece and Dragon Ball, which called for stronger government action on anime piracy.

According to data published by Japan’s Ministry of Economy, Trade, and Industry, piracy losses from digital content rose from two trillion yen in 2022 to 5.7 trillion yen in 2025, increasing from roughly $13.3 billion to around $38 billion USD.

In a bid to curb those losses, Japan’s Agency for Cultural Affairs has also expanded its AI piracy tests to target overseas sites hosting unauthorized copies of manga and anime, with plans to compile its findings as early as March 2027.
